cim: The Grid Under Siege: How AI Is Creating New Risks to America’s Energy Infrastructure
cim_eredeti: The Grid Under Siege: How AI Is Creating New Risks to America’s Energy Infrastructure
szoveg_eredeti:
Chuck Brooks is the president of Brooks Consulting International and one of Executive Mosaic’s GovCon Experts.

AI is altering the threat landscape by enabling adversaries to see more of the grid, comprehend its weaknesses and devise attack plans more quickly than conventional defenses can react. The energy grid is growing more sophisticated, networked and reliant on artificial intelligence. Increased efficiency, predictive maintenance, better energy distribution and the capacity to handle increasingly complicated power demands are all promised by these developments. However, they are also establishing a brand-new, possibly hazardous cybersecurity environment.

I have written extensively about critical infrastructure vulnerabilities, particularly in relation to the convergence of information technology, artificial intelligence, operational technology, or OT, and the Internet of Things, or IoT. One of my concerns for a long time has been the inability to distinguish between the security of the energy grid and the security of the digital networks, devices and communications systems that are connected to it. The urgency of that issue is growing.

Adversaries are able to map interconnected systems, conduct surveillance, find vulnerabilities and create complex exploitation strategies thanks to artificial intelligence. AI-assisted reconnaissance and automated cyber operations are increasingly able to accomplish tasks that previously required specialized technical knowledge, significant resources and a significant amount of time.

Hackers trying to break into a utility’s corporate network are not the only ones who pose a threat. It is the capacity of highly skilled adversaries to comprehend the larger digital ecosystem that surrounds the grid, pinpoint its weakest links and possibly exploit those links to interfere with actual operations. AI is altering the threat landscape by enabling adversaries to see more of the grid, comprehend its weaknesses and devise attack plans more quickly than conventional defenses can react.

As adversaries use AI to target the energy grid and defenders turn to AI to protect it, the Potomac Officers Club’s 2027 Artificial Intelligence Summit on March 18 will explore securing critical infrastructure in the AI era. Save your seat now!

Power plants, transmission lines, substations and distribution networks are no longer the only components of the modern electric grid. This cyber-physical ecosystem is intricate. Nearly every layer of the energy infrastructure is now connected by digital technologies. Utilities are assisted in monitoring and controlling the production and distribution of electricity by intelligent electronic devices, smart meters, sensors, automated grid-management platforms, industrial control systems, SCADA systems, PLCs and intelligent electronic devices.

An additional level of complexity is introduced by the switch to renewable energy. Additional linked devices and control systems are introduced by solar installations, wind farms, battery storage, distributed energy resources, infrastructure for charging electric vehicles and microgrids. Although these technologies increase efficiency, a potential vulnerability may be introduced by each connection. In addition, the grid relies on third-party vendors, software providers, cloud services, telecommunications networks and remote maintenance systems. An adversary may be able to gain indirect access to a more vulnerable system if one of these interconnected environments is compromised.

The fact that many energy operators continue to use outdated equipment that was created decades ago, when connectivity and remote access were not major design factors, makes this especially troubling. As a result, the infrastructure is becoming more interconnected, making it possible for one organization’s security to rely on that of dozens or even hundreds of other organizations.

The use of AI to carry out advanced surveillance and reconnaissance against energy infrastructure is one of the biggest new risks. Historically, adversaries have used human intelligence, network scanning, open-source research and extended observation to obtain intelligence about critical infrastructure. AI significantly increases the potential scope and effectiveness of those endeavors.

Large amounts of publicly accessible data can be processed by generative AI and autonomous agents, which can also create comprehensive intelligence profiles and determine connections between infrastructure and organizations. Think about what an adversary could discover by merging data from publicly available network information, employee profiles, job postings, infrastructure maps, satellite imagery, equipment specifications, vendor portals, public utility documents and regulatory filings.

These sources might not provide much information on their own. When combined and examined by AI, they could offer a far more comprehensive view of the technology environment, suppliers, remote-access dependencies and possible vulnerabilities of an energy operator.

AI can also be used to find patterns in operational data, correlate past outages, identify equipment dependencies and rank infrastructure components or organizations for additional research. This represents a novel aspect of digital surveillance. Initial network penetration is not always necessary. Before attempting an intrusion, an adversary might be able to gather useful intelligence. Combining AI-assisted reconnaissance with ongoing access to cloud, telecom, and other third-party networks raises even more concerns.

This is important, as the Volt Typhoon campaign proved. China-affiliated actors attempted to pre-position themselves within vital infrastructure networks, possibly creating access that could be used during a future geopolitical crisis, according to warnings from U.S. government agencies. Such activity does not always aim to cause an immediate disruption. It might be to comprehend networks, keep access and maintain the capacity to act when it is strategically advantageous. This kind of preparation and reconnaissance could be made quicker, more thorough and harder to spot with AI.

AI-enabled threats to operational technology are real, as evidenced by recent government warnings. Cyber actors were conducting targeted reconnaissance and creating AI-generated exploitation scripts against Siemens S7 programmable logic controllers used in U.S. critical infrastructure, according to a cybersecurity advisory released by the National Security Agency and partner agencies in August 2026. See: AI-generated exploitation scripts targeting Siemens PLCs in U.S. critical infrastructure.

The scripts were passed off as genuine monitoring instruments. Energy production and distribution, manufacturing, water and wastewater treatment, chemical processing and other vital industries were among the impacted sectors. The agencies issued a warning that improperly protected controllers could be exploited to disrupt industrial processes, damage equipment, result in safety incidents and have cascading effects on interconnected systems.

Since PLCs are directly involved in managing physical processes, this is a significant development. An IT security incident is not the same as a compromise of an inadequately secured controller. Physical operations may be impacted, depending on the attack and the system. The caution also demonstrates how AI can reduce the technical obstacles to creating tools that communicate with industrial systems.

CISA, the FBI and other government partners revised their advisory in July 2026 regarding cyber actors with ties to Iran that target internet-connected programmable logic controllers. Siemens, Schneider Electric and Rockwell Automation were added to the list of manufacturers targeted by the revised warning.
